status.text: As of the Senate floor log for Nov. 12, the Senate had adopted the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347 and cloture motions on the Capito substitute (SA 6883) and on the bill were set to ripen at 5:30 p.m. Monday, Nov. 16.

source.label: U.S. Senate Daily Press, Thursday, November 12, 2026

status.quote: Finally, that the cloture motions filed during Wednesday’s session of the Senate ripen at 5:30 p.m. on Monday, November 16th.

status.text: Per Senate records as reported by WLJ, neither the Nov. 9 cloture vote nor the Nov. 10 motion-to-proceed vote was final passage of the bill.
status.quote: Senators voted 62-21 Nov. 10 to begin consideration of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), following a 73-25 procedural vote Nov. 9. Neither vote constituted final passage, according to Senate records.

items.author: Chuck Schumer
items.title: Leader Schumer Statement After Permitting Reform Bill Advances In The Senate
items.summary: Schumer said he is voting to move the debate forward despite outstanding concerns with parts of the bill that he will seek to address through amendments. He credited Sens. Whitehouse and Heinrich.

quote.text: While I have outstanding concerns with parts of the bill that I’ll fight to address through the amendment process, I’m voting today to move this debate forward.
quote.speaker: Chuck Schumer, Democratic Leader, U.S. Senate

items.outlet: Office of Sen. Edward J. Markey
items.author: Edward J. Markey
items.title: Senator Markey Statement on Permitting Reform Deal
items.summary: Markey said he will vote against the motion to invoke cloture, citing timing, transparency, and threats to clean air, water and Tribes.

quote.text: Because of these issues on timing, transparency, and threats to our clean air, water, and Tribes, I will vote against the motion to invoke cloture on this legislation.
quote.speaker: Edward J. Markey, U.S. Senator (D-Mass.)

items.author: Jeff Merkley
items.title: Sen. Merkley Statement on Senate Permitting Legislation
items.summary: Merkley said he supports the transmission and data-center cost provisions, said the bill accelerates fossil fuel extraction, and said he will vote against the bill before the Senate.

quote.text: But the current bill raises too many serious issues that require more deliberation. I will vote against the bill before us today, but I look forward to working with my colleagues to get permitting reform right.
quote.speaker: Jeff Merkley, U.S. Senator (D-Ore.)

items.author: Tim Kaine
items.title: Kaine Statement on Permitting Reform Legislation
items.summary: Kaine said he is voting against the procedural motion over changes to the National Historic Preservation Act and will seek amendments that could lead him to support the bill.

quote.text: For this reason, I am voting against today’s procedural motion. I will seek to amend the bill to address my concerns and, if successful, could support it with appropriate changes.
quote.speaker: Tim Kaine, U.S. Senator (D-Va.)

items.outlet: Office of Sen. Chris Van Hollen
items.author: Chris Van Hollen
items.title: Van Hollen Statement on Current Opposition to Moving Forward with Permitting Reform Legislation
items.summary: Van Hollen said he voted against moving forward, citing offshore wind and Chesapeake Bay provisions, and said he is putting forward changes.

quote.text: I’m putting forward changes to the bill to address these concerns; however, while I support the goal behind tackling our burdensome and outdated permitting system, given this bill’s impact on Maryland, I cannot support it in its current form.
quote.speaker: Chris Van Hollen, U.S. Senator (D-Md.)

items.author: Michael Bennet
items.title: Bennet Statement on Permitting Reform Vote
items.summary: Bennet said he voted against advancing the bill, citing protection of Tribal cultural resources and changes to public engagement, and that he wants the bill vetted more thoroughly.

quote.text: These changes must be vetted more thoroughly before passing into law. Given these concerns, I cannot support advancing this bill at this time.
quote.speaker: Michael Bennet, U.S. Senator (D-Colo.)

items.author: Alan Armstrong
items.title: Senator Armstrong Praises Senate Vote to Advance Landmark Bipartisan Permitting Reform Legislation
items.summary: Armstrong said the 73-25 cloture vote on the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347 was a major step and urged the Senate to pass the bill.

quote.text: Tonight’s vote marks a major step forward. I applaud my colleagues on both sides of the aisle for coming together to advance meaningful permitting reforms
quote.speaker: Alan Armstrong, U.S. Senator (R-Okla.)

items.author: Fred Krupp
items.title: Statement: Senate to hold initial vote on permitting bill
items.summary: EDF's president said the latest version contains reforms to get clean energy on the grid and also unwinds protections for air, water and communities, and that the group wants improvements before final passage.

quote.text: The latest version has important reforms to get clean energy on the grid and upgrade our aging infrastructure, but it also unwinds protections for our air, water and communities,
quote.speaker: Fred Krupp, President, Environmental Defense Fund

items.title: Rounds is lone Republican vote against permitting reform, noting state-level concerns
items.summary: SDPB reports that Rounds was the only Republican to vote against the cloture motion and cited, in a Facebook post, landowners' ability to negotiate with state and local stakeholders before federal intervention.

quote.text: South Dakota landowners deserve to negotiate with stakeholders at the state and local level before federal intervention is required,
quote.speaker: Mike Rounds, U.S. Senator (R-S.D.)

items.author: Mike Lee
items.title: Congressional Record, Senate, November 10, 2026 (floor remarks, permitting reform)
items.summary: Lee's floor remarks on permitting reform state that current permitting processes delay energy projects and that more energy on the grid is needed.

quote.text: Today, a company can spend years trying to get permission just to build a powerplant, and a transmission line
quote.speaker: Mike Lee, U.S. Senator (R-Utah)

items.title: How they voted, Nov. 15, 2026
items.summary: The roundup reports the Nov. 9 cloture vote, lists the New Mexico delegation's votes, and quotes Capito as a supporter of the bill.

quote.text: creates predictability, consistency, and finality in securing a permit. And it will allow our laws to balance public health, the environment, and the needs of our economy.
quote.speaker: Shelley Moore Capito, U.S. Senator (R-W.Va.), as quoted by the Santa Fe New Mexican

items.author: Mara Hoplamazian
items.title: Senators Advance Bipartisan Permitting Reform. Democrats Were Divided.
items.summary: The report lists Democrats who voted no on the Nov. 9 cloture vote and the reasons given, including Duckworth's concern about presidential power and Luján's citation of tribal concerns.

quote.text: Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) voted no, saying she was concerned the package could hand Trump more power.
quote.speaker: Mara Hoplamazian, reporter, The Washington Sun

items.author: Charles Wallace
items.title: Senate advances bill overhauling federal permitting rules
items.summary: The article reports the 73-25 cloture vote on Nov. 9 and the 62-21 vote on Nov. 10, notes that neither was final passage, and says the Nov. 7 substitute was released by Lee, Capito, Heinrich and Whitehouse.

quote.text: Senators voted 62-21 Nov. 10 to begin consideration of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), following a 73-25 procedural vote Nov. 9. Neither vote constituted final passage, according to Senate records.
quote.speaker: Charles Wallace, reporter, Western Livestock Journal

items.author: Michael Bommarito
items.title: BAAJA’s First Senate Vote: Who Voted Yes, Who Voted No
items.summary: The consultancy's roll-call comparison, updated Nov. 11, compares roll calls 257 and 258 and lists the senators who did not vote on one or the other.

quote.text: No senator switched sides. Roll calls 257 and 258 differ for 17 senators. Every difference involves a senator who did not vote in one of the two roll calls.
quote.speaker: Michael Bommarito, Bommarito Consulting
